sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Let's explore the world of true/false values in programming! Booleans are like light switches - they're either ON (true) or OFF (false).

• What boolean data types are and why they matter
• How to compare values using relational operators
• Where you'll use booleans in real code

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Imagine you're at a traffic light. It's either RED (stop - false) or GREEN (go - true). That's exactly how booleans work in programming!

Booleans are the simplest data type - they can only be:
• `true` (yes, on, 1)
• `false` (no, off, 0)

They're perfect for answering yes/no questions like:
- Is the user logged in?
- Is the password correct?
- Has the game started?

sections.title: Code Examples
Key Points
points: A boolean variable can hold only two values: true or false
Use == to compare values; do not confuse with = which is assignment
Boolean expressions are used as conditions in if statements and loops
Boolean variables are useful for storing the result of a condition for later use

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: Booleans are simple true/false values that power decisions in code. Relational operators compare values and return booleans. Practice using them in conditions and flags.

questions.question: What are the two possible values of a boolean variable in Java?
questions.explanation: In Java, the boolean data type has exactly two possible values: true and false. Unlike some languages, Java does not allow 0 and 1 to represent boolean values.

questions.question: What is the result of the expression: 5 > 3?
questions.explanation: The comparison operator > returns a boolean value. Since 5 is greater than 3, the expression 5 > 3 evaluates to true.
